The query is scoped to this Dag and this run, so it cannot see a row recorded against any other Dag or any other run.
Rows with a null `dag_id` are unreachable by a dag_id-scoped query and need a separate fleet-wide audit-log permission, so this reading never covers them.
The `log` table is cleanable by `airflow db clean` (utils/db_cleanup.py:189, included when `--tables` is omitted), so an empty history can also mean retention removed the rows.

`cli_*` rows are written with NO `run_id` at all - the CLI action logger inserts only event, owner, extra, task_id, dag_id and logical_date (utils/cli_action_loggers.py:133-146, off the metrics built at utils/cli.py:210-224) - so `run_id` is null on every one of them and a run-scoped query structurally cannot return any. That includes `cli_dag_test`, the `airflow dags test --mark-success-pattern` route named in the unknowns above: a CLI-driven state change is invisible to this reading whether or not it happened.

`extra` is projected to the four keys this tool reads (`method`, `new_state`, `task_ids`, `map_index`) and only for the HEADLINE row of each task instance; every other key is named in `extra_keys` and withheld, and the context rows under `events` carry no `extra` at all. Airflow masks `extra` by key NAME only, so relaying it whole passed through anything the requester chose to call something else.

The attribution payload is bounded at runtime, not only by the per-field clamps: the serialized `last_state_change` objects are measured and, past the ceiling reported in `attribution_payload_limit`, context rows and then `extra` projections are dropped from the oldest instances first. Any row that lost content says so with `size_reduced`, and the count is in `attribution_reduced_for_size`.

normalized_result.source:
"""Gate 0 fixture (R2 replacement): a task ADDED mid-run by version drift.

Version 1 of this file (the one this run is triggered against) contains the
chain ``stage_extract >> stage_transform >> stage_publish`` and nothing else.
While a run is in flight, ``stage_reconcile`` is inserted between
``stage_transform`` and ``stage_publish`` and the bundle is reserialized, so the
run's scheduler loop sees a task that did not exist when the run started.

The point of the fixture is to observe what Airflow does with that new task:
whether the resulting task instance can ever carry the forged signature
(``try_number == 0``, empty ``hostname``, null ``pid`` / ``queued_when`` /
``scheduled_when``) while reading ``success``.

Ordering-only wiring (``>>``, no XCom hand-off) so that inserting a task into
the middle of the chain does not break a data dependency.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import time

import pendulum

from airflow.sdk import DAG, task


@task
def stage_extract() -> None:
    """Long on purpose: this is the window in which version 2 is serialized."""
    for tick in range(180):
        time.sleep(1)
        if tick % 30 == 0:
            print(f"extracting settlement rows, {tick}s elapsed")
    print("extract complete")


@task
def stage_transform() -> None:
    for tick in range(60):
        time.sleep(1)
        if tick % 20 == 0:
            print(f"transforming settlement rows, {tick}s elapsed")
    print("transform complete")


@task
def stage_reconcile() -> None:
    """Added in version 2, while run ``gate0_drift_001`` was already in flight."""
    time.sleep(10)
    print("settlement reconciled against the ledger")


@task
def stage_publish() -> None:
    time.sleep(5)
    print("settlement published")


with DAG(
    dag_id="gate0_drift_reconcile",
    schedule=None,
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    catchup=False,
    tags=["gate0"],
):
    stage_extract() >> stage_transform() >> stage_reconcile() >> stage_publish()
